title: The prayer settles in
hook: after long practice, the pilgrim finds the prayer running on its own with his heartbeat
tomorrow: what do you give when your hands are empty?

segments.voice: Yesterday a man heard pray without ceasing and walked until an elder showed him how: how to pray always? Today, deep into the practice, something changes.
screen: `HOW TO PRAY ALWAYS?` → `DEEP INTO THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: There's a rhythm in your chest that kept going through every class, every argument, every night of sleep, and never once needed a reminder. The pilgrim in The Way of a Pilgrim learns to set a prayer to that beat. It doesn't start there. At first it's work. He says the Jesus Prayer over and over, as his elder told him, and some days it's dull; his tongue keeps going while his mind wanders off. Then one morning he wakes, and the prayer is already going, before he's decided to start.
screen: `A RHYTHM THAT NEVER NEEDS A REMINDER.` → `AT FIRST, IT'S WORK.` → `HE WAKES, AND IT'S ALREADY GOING.`

segments.voice: The elder gives him a daily task, and he keeps it: Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me, on the road, at meals, in the evening. After a while, he says, the prayer starts to move. It begins on his lips. Then it seems to slip down into his heart. Later, reading the Philokalia, he learns a way to join the words to his heartbeat, one word to each beat. Lord on one. Jesus on the next. Christ on the next. And to let the words ride the breath, in and out. Then comes the part this lesson is named for. The prayer, he says, seemed to pray by itself. It went on while he walked, while he talked with people, even, he says, while he slept. Here's a line to tell a friend tonight, from the Song of Songs, that fits his picture: “I sleep, but my heart waketh.” The body rests; something underneath keeps watch. It's worth saying what the book doesn't promise. It never calls this quick. He learned it under an elder's guidance, and some Orthodox teachers warn against forcing breath or heartbeat methods alone. The prayer settles in the way a path gets worn into a field: by walking it, again and again, until the feet find it on their own.
screen: `FROM THE LIPS TO THE HEART.` · `ONE WORD TO EACH BEAT.` · `I SLEEP, BUT MY HEART WAKETH.` · `NOT QUICK, AND NOT ALONE.` · then, large: `THE PRAYER PRAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Find your pulse, at the wrist or the side of the neck, or rest a hand flat on your chest until you feel the beat. Don't change it; just follow it. The pilgrim set Lord, Jesus, Christ on three beats. You can do the same, or simply count the beats in threes, and let your breath go at its own pace.
The prayer settles in. Said again and again, until it moves from the lips to the heart and seems to go on by itself.
Pocket this one: the prayer prays itself. He didn't start there; he started with work. Day sixteen seventy, done.

screen: `DAY 1670 COUNTS.` → `SAINTS AND TEACHERS IN THEIR OWN WORDS · 69 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DO YOU GIVE WITH EMPTY HANDS?`

howItsDone: Some Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer slowly with a prayer rope, sometimes in time with the breath, ideally with guidance from an experienced spiritual father or mother.

chat.says: dress rehearsal tonight. my heart is POUNDING. how am i supposed to pray when i can't even calm down?
options: Use the pounding. Let a short prayer ride the beat, one word each, like the pilgrim.
Calm down first. The pilgrim only prayed once his heart was still and slow.
Skip praying tonight. It only works when it runs by itself, without effort.
chat.meaning: The pilgrim joined the prayer's words to his heartbeat, and with long practice it seemed to pray itself. The beat you already have is a place to start.

Jesus Prayer.meaning: the short prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me

Philokalia.meaning: an old collection of Orthodox writings on prayer

elder.meaning: an experienced monk who guides others in prayer

Song of Songs.meaning: a book of love poems in the Bible, also called the Song of Solomon
